uncited: This family applies Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) to tomographic reconstruction, replacing discrete voxel grids with continuous functions parameterized by neural networks [S1, unofficial].

It solves the ill-posed inverse problem of recovering 3D density fields from sparse, noisy, or limited-angle X-ray projections by leveraging the differentiability of the rendering pipeline [S1, unofficial].

Unlike traditional discrete methods, these approaches optimize network weights directly, allowing for high-resolution reconstruction from minimal data and enabling simultaneous self-calibration of geometric and photometric parameters [S1].
where $R(x)$ is a regularizer (e.g., Total Variation, neural prior) and $\lambda$ is a weighting factor [S1, unofficial][S2].
**Forward Projection:** Ray marching through the volume representation (voxels, octrees, or neural fields) to compute line integrals of density/absorption coefficients [S1, unofficial].
**Backward Projection (Adjoint):** Distributing the error from the 2D detector plane back into the 3D volume.

**Optimization Loop:** An iterative process (e.g., SGD, Adam) that updates the volume parameters (voxel values, neural network weights, or Gaussian parameters) to reduce the projection error [S1, unofficial][S2].
The application of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) to X-ray tomography emerged from the success of NeRF in novel view synthesis for visible light [S1, unofficial].
Traditional iterative reconstruction methods (e.g., SIRT, FDK) struggle with sparse data and noise [S1].
Neural inverse rendering methods were developed to leverage the continuous nature of INRs for higher resolution and robustness in ill-posed scenarios [S1, unofficial].
